summaries.example: Imagine you are drawing a picture of a castle. The castle is not really in the room, but your mind can make it seem present in an imagined world. Sartre thought this ability shows that people can step back from what is here and think about what could be different. That freedom also means we must choose how to respond to our situation.
summaries.summary: Jean-Paul Sartre was a French philosopher and writer who explored consciousness, imagination, freedom, responsibility, and our relationships with other people. He used phenomenology, a careful study of experience, to argue that consciousness reaches toward the world rather than containing a fixed inner object called the self. He said imagination can show us things as absent or unreal, and that this ability helps us see that the world could be different. Sartre described objects as simply being what they are, while people can question, refuse, plan, and change. Because people are always in a real situation, freedom does not mean being able to do anything at all. It means that a situation does not completely choose our response for us. Sartre called it bad faith when someone treats a role or label as if it were the whole truth about them. He also studied shame and the experience of being seen by another person. His books, plays, and political writings brought these ideas to a wide public, while his arguments about race, colonialism, society, and collective action remain subjects of discussion.
key_ideas: Our minds are usually focused on things in the world, not on a permanent little self hidden inside us.
Imagination lets us think about things that are absent, fictional, or not yet real.
People are always in situations, but a situation does not completely decide what they will do.
We can treat ourselves as more than a job, label, past mistake, or other person’s opinion.
Sartre connected philosophy with novels, plays, political writing, and public action.
summaries.why_it_matters: Sartre’s ideas invite us to notice how we experience the world and how we take responsibility for our choices. They can help us ask whether a label describes us completely, whether we are avoiding a difficult choice, and how other people’s views affect us. His work also shows that philosophy can appear in stories, plays, art, and public debates.

important_terms.definition: A way of studying conscious experience by carefully describing how things appear to us.
The fact that consciousness is always directed toward something, such as a tree, a memory, or an imagined castle.
Sartre’s name for pretending that we are only a fixed role, label, or situation and cannot choose how to respond.
The idea that people are not born with one finished purpose; they make themselves through choices and actions.

questions_to_think_about: Can a person be more than a label such as “student,” “friend,” or “athlete”?
How is imagining a dragon different from seeing a real dog?
If a difficult situation does not decide everything, what choices might still be possible?
When might someone be hiding from their freedom?

summaries.example: Suppose a student is exhausted during a difficult hike. The fatigue is a fact about the student’s body, but it does not by itself determine whether the student rests, continues, asks for help, or changes the goal. The student interprets the fatigue within a situation and a project. Sartre would say that freedom is not unlimited power; it is the capacity to take up facts through possible ends and actions.
summaries.summary:
Jean-Paul Sartre’s philosophy joins phenomenology with existential questions about freedom, responsibility, imagination, and other people. His early work argues that intentional consciousness is not a container holding a permanent Ego. In ordinary, pre-reflective experience, consciousness is absorbed in an object or activity; reflection can then make an experience or an Ego into an object, but the reflected Ego is not identical with the subject of the original experience. In The Imaginary, Sartre argues that imagining differs from perceiving because the imagined object is given as absent, unreal, or fictional. This ability to ‘irrealize’ the present helps explain how consciousness can take a position toward the world and imagine alternatives.

In Being and Nothingness, Sartre distinguishes being-in-itself, the plenitude of objects, from being-for-itself, conscious existence. The for-itself is defined by negation: it can encounter an absence, see a situation as lacking something, and project a future possibility. From this, Sartre develops a radical but situated account of freedom. A person never chooses without bodily, social, historical, and material conditions, yet those conditions do not mechanically dictate the meaning of an action. Freedom is realized in projects and conduct, not merely in private intention. ‘Bad faith’ names attempts to deny this structure by treating oneself as nothing more than a fixed identity or, conversely, as pure freedom without facts.

Sartre also analyzes the Look, shame, and the experience of becoming an object for another consciousness. Later work develops existential psychoanalysis, which interprets conduct through a person’s fundamental project rather than through a purely causal unconscious. key_ideas: Sartre distinguishes being-in-itself from being-for-itself: objects are presented as what they are, while consciousness can negate, question, and project possibilities.
Pre-reflective consciousness is already directed toward the world; reflective consciousness can make an experience or an Ego its object, but does not reveal a permanent inner substance.
Imagination presents its object as absent, nonexistent, or fictional. This ‘irrealizing’ capacity is connected with freedom because it allows consciousness to stand back from the given world.
Freedom is situated. Facts such as bodily limits, social conditions, and the past matter, but their significance depends on how a person takes them up in a project.
Bad faith is not simply lying to another person. It is an unstable attempt to deny either one’s freedom to transcend a situation or the facts that constrain one’s life.
The Look of another person can disclose us as beings-for-others and produce shame; Sartre’s early account presents conflict as central to human relations, though his views are debated.
summaries.why_it_matters: Sartre matters because he offers a demanding account of agency that avoids two simple extremes: people are neither completely unconstrained nor merely products of circumstances. His analyses connect first-person experience with questions about self-knowledge, social recognition, artistic creation, and responsibility. His later discussions of groups, racism, colonialism, and historical conditions also show how a philosophy centered on individual freedom can be extended toward collective life, even though scholars debate how successfully the early and later views fit together.

important_terms.definition: Sartre’s method of describing lived experience, especially how objects, other people, and possibilities appear before theoretical explanation.
The directedness of consciousness toward an object, whether the object is perceived, remembered, desired, or imagined.
Being that is full and simply is what it is; Sartre uses this mainly for objects, in contrast with conscious existence.
Conscious existence, characterized by distance from what is given, negation, projects, and the ability to transcend a current situation.
A way consciousness brings absence, difference, lack, or possibility into experience rather than merely registering positive facts.
A self-deceptive pattern in which someone identifies exclusively with facticity, transcendence, or a socially assigned role.
The idea that the kind of person one becomes is not fixed in advance but develops through existence, choices, and projects.
Sartre’s account of understanding a person through the organizing project that gives meaning to many of their actions, without reducing them to mechanical causes.

questions_to_think_about: Does recognizing that a situation has several possible meanings prove that a person is free?
Can a social role be lived responsibly without becoming an example of bad faith?
Is Sartre right that reflection cannot simply discover a fixed self inside consciousness?
Does the experience of being watched reveal another person directly, or only our fear of being judged?
How might Sartre’s account of freedom change when social structures and historical conditions are emphasized?

summaries.example: A new student may think, “Everyone sees me as the quiet kid, so I cannot speak up.” Sartre would say the student’s past behavior and the opinions of others are real facts, but they do not completely define the student. The student can choose a project, such as joining a discussion or helping a classmate, and thereby act beyond the old label. That choice may be difficult, but it is still made within a situation.
summaries.summary:
Jean-Paul Sartre was a major French philosopher, novelist, playwright, and public intellectual. He is associated with existentialism, a philosophical approach that examines human freedom, responsibility, meaning, and life in a particular situation. Sartre’s starting point was phenomenology: instead of beginning with a theory about the mind, he described how objects, absences, imagined things, and other people are experienced.

Sartre adopted the idea of intentionality, according to which consciousness is always directed toward something. When someone is absorbed in catching a bus or looking at a painting, they may not be thinking about a separate inner self at all. Sartre therefore challenged the idea of a permanent Ego standing behind every experience. He distinguished immediate, pre-reflective awareness from reflection, in which a person turns an experience into something to examine. The self found in reflection is an object of consciousness, not a hidden substance that explains every experience.

Sartre also argued that imagination differs from perception. A perceived object belongs to the shared world, while an imagined character or place is presented as absent, fictional, or unreal. Because imagination can move beyond what is currently given, Sartre connects it with freedom and with artistic creation.

In Being and Nothingness, Sartre contrasts being-in-itself with being-for-itself. Objects simply are what they are. Consciousness, by contrast, can notice what is missing, reject a description, remember the past, and project a future. This ability to introduce distance and possibility is called negation. key_ideas: Sartre says consciousness is directed outward toward the world, not built around a permanent inner Ego that can be found like an object.
Imagination is different from perception because it gives us an absent, fictional, or unreal object, and this helps us think beyond what is immediately present.
Freedom does not mean unlimited choice. It means that people interpret and respond to their facts through projects, even when their options are restricted.
Bad faith happens when someone treats a role or identity as a solid thing that leaves no room for choice, or pretends to be free while ignoring real circumstances.
Other people affect how we understand ourselves. Sartre uses the Look and shame to explain how we can suddenly experience ourselves as seen and judged.
Sartre later connected existential freedom with groups, history, economic conditions, racism, colonialism, and political action.
summaries.why_it_matters: Sartre’s philosophy helps explain why people can feel both shaped by circumstances and responsible for their responses. It gives useful language for thinking about labels, peer pressure, shame, self-deception, creative imagination, and political responsibility. His work also encourages readers to connect private choices with the social and historical worlds in which those choices become possible.

important_terms.definition: The careful study of how experiences appear from a person’s point of view, before explaining them with scientific or abstract theories.
The idea that consciousness is always consciousness of something: a real object, a feeling, a memory, a goal, or an imagined thing.
The part of reality that simply is what it is, like an object that does not question or plan its own existence.
Conscious human existence, which can question the present, imagine alternatives, and take a stand toward its circumstances.
The capacity to recognize absence, difference, lack, or a possibility that is not yet real.
A way of avoiding freedom by acting as though a role, label, or situation completely determines who one is.
Sartre’s claim that people develop their identity through living and choosing rather than receiving a complete purpose at birth.
Sartre’s account of interpreting a life through a broad project that connects many actions and choices.

questions_to_think_about: Can a person be responsible for a choice when their choices are heavily limited?
Why might Sartre think imagining a fictional world is connected with freedom?
Is accepting a role always bad faith, or does the problem arise only when the role is treated as the whole self?
How can another person’s attention change the way you experience yourself?
Do groups become freer when people act together, or can organized groups create new forms of control?
